h1:
Songkhla Tao Kua
The Local Dish with Toddy Palm Sugar Dressing
intro: Tao kua is one of those dishes you simply can't get anywhere else — and that's what makes it worth seeking out. It looks a bit like a salad or a vermicelli yam, but the soul of the dish is the dressing: toddy palm sugar that delivers sweet, salty, and sour all in one spoonful. It sits on a bed of blanched rice vermicelli, bean sprouts, fried tofu, crispy whole prawns, and shrimp crackers. Locals in Songkhla have been eating it for breakfast and lunch for generations. We break down exactly what's in it, why the palm sugar matters, and the 10 spots where people actually go back for more.
chips: 🦐 Fried tofu · shrimp crackers · crispy prawns

blocks.html: Ask any local what food truly belongs to Songkhla and tao kua comes up fast. It's hard to find outside the area because the whole dish depends on the dressing — made from fresh toddy palm sugar and palm vinegar sourced from palms around Songkhla Lake. That natural sweetness has a depth that ordinary sugar just can't replicate. Locals half-jokingly call it the "lakeside salad." It's mild, not spicy at all, making it a rare relief for anyone nervous about the bold flavours of Southern Thai food.

blocks.text: What Is Tao Kua? What Goes in It?

blocks.html: Tao kua is a one-plate dish that falls somewhere between a yam (Thai-style salad) and a composed plate. A single serving layers at least 8–9 components together. The fun is in the contrast: soft, crunchy, and chewy all in one bite. The moment you toss everything with the dressing, the flavours round out completely.

items: Blanched rice vermicelli + bean sprouts — the base of the dish; the silky noodles and crisp sprouts soak up the dressing beautifully
Fried tofu — yellow tofu sliced and fried until the outside is golden and the inside stays soft; it's the star ingredient that gives the dish its name (tao kua = fried tofu in Hokkien)
Shrimp crackers — fried and scattered on top for crunch and a gentle prawn aroma; some shops crush them coarsely and toss them through the dressing
Crispy whole prawns — small prawns deep-fried shell-on until completely crisp; addictively snackable and fragrant
Boiled pork, pork ear, and head meat — thinly sliced boiled pork and pig ear for a rich, slightly chewy bite; some shops add sliced blood tofu too
Soft-boiled duck egg — yolk still just a little runny, which cuts through the richness of the fried elements
Blanched water spinach + cucumber — fresh and lightly cooked vegetables that keep the plate from feeling heavy

blocks.title: Good to know before you order
blocks.html: Most shops offer two versions: mixed (everything already tossed in dressing) and separate (dressing on the side so you control how much goes in). If you like things crispy without going soggy, ask for separate — you get to manage the texture yourself. Most shops also do takeaway bags, handy if you want to eat while walking around the Old Town.

blocks.text: Why Does It Have to Be Toddy Palm Sugar?

blocks.html: What separates Songkhla tao kua from a generic vermicelli salad is the dressing. Old-school shops simmer toddy palm sugar and palm vinegar sourced from the palms growing around Songkhla Lake — the result is a naturally sweet, fragrant depth that regular white sugar simply can't produce. Combined with a touch of salt or fish sauce and a souring agent, the dressing hits three notes: sweet up front, salty in the middle, sour to finish. The moment it coats the crispy fried ingredients, everything comes together. That's why people say tao kua from outside Songkhla never quite tastes the same.

That sweetness is also why tao kua works for people who can't handle spice or rich Southern Thai food. Kids and older family members eat it comfortably. Anyone who wants heat can always ask for dried chilli flakes or chilli vinegar on the side.

blocks.text: 10 Tao Kua Spots Locals in Songkhla and Hat Yai Actually Go To

blocks.html: We pulled this list from genuine review patterns and places that locals return to regularly — a mix of long-running shops in Songkhla Old Town and stalls inside Hat Yai markets. Prices are per-plate estimates and can shift with ingredient costs and the time of year. Many shops sell only from morning until early afternoon and take regular days off. It's worth a quick check with the shop before you make a special trip.

items.name: Tao Kua Pa Iad (Nang Ngam Rd, Songkhla Old Town)
items.blurb: A long-running tao kua shop in a shophouse on Nang Ngam Road, right in the middle of Songkhla Old Town. The dressing uses toddy palm sugar and palm vinegar for a traditionally rounded sweetness. The plate comes fully loaded — fried tofu, crispy prawns, pig ear, soft-boiled egg. It's a regular stop for visitors exploring the Old Town.
items.meta: Nang Ngam Rd, Songkhla Old Town · open approx. 9:00–13:30

items.name: Pa Juab Thao Kua (Soi Yaring entrance, Nang Ngam Rd)
items.blurb: A Songkhla Old Town institution. This shop has been selling tao kua alongside pork bone noodles for years, at the entrance to Soi Yaring on Nang Ngam Road. It gets packed — especially in the mornings. The tao kua comes loaded and the palm sugar dressing hits hard. It's the first name most Songkhla locals think of.
items.meta: Soi Yaring entrance, Nang Ngam Rd · open morning–early afternoon

items.name: Tao Kua Pa Taew (Kim Yong Market, Hat Yai)
items.blurb: The go-to tao kua name inside Kim Yong Market in central Hat Yai. Sold in takeaway bags so you can eat while browsing the market. The palm sugar dressing is smooth and fragrant; the price is very easy on the wallet. A natural pit stop when you're shopping for souvenirs.
items.meta: Kim Yong Market, Hat Yai · open morning–early afternoon

items.name: Tao Kua Pa Iad Branch 2 (Khlong R.5 canal, Hat Yai)
items.blurb: The Hat Yai branch of the Pa Iad recipe, on the Khlong R.5 canal. More open and relaxed than the Old Town original. Uses the same palm sugar dressing. The right choice if you're staying in Hat Yai and don't want to make the trip into Songkhla.
items.meta: Khlong R.5 canal, Hat Yai · open morning–early afternoon

items.name: Tao Kua Jeh Eng (Samchai Rd, Hat Yai)
items.blurb: One of Hat Yai's own long-standing tao kua spots, on Samchai Road. Locals in the area have been eating here for years. The palm sugar dressing is sweet and fragrant, the fried tofu is properly crispy outside and soft inside, and it's a regular weekday lunch for people working nearby.
items.meta: Samchai Rd, Hat Yai · open morning–early afternoon

items.name: Tao Kua Pa Taew Branch 2 (Hat Yai)
items.blurb: The second Hat Yai location running Pa Taew's original recipe. Offers both takeaway bags and sit-down. The palm sugar dressing holds the same consistent flavour as the Kim Yong Market flagship. A good call if you want the Pa Taew taste without dealing with market crowds.

items.name: Tao Kua Nam Tan Tonad — Pa Iad Recipe (Hat Yai)
items.blurb: A shop that leads with its toddy palm sugar dressing as the main selling point. Fresh ingredients throughout — tofu and prawns fried to order. Reviewers praise the sweetness as fragrant without being cloying. Worth a try if you lean toward the sweeter, more aromatic style.

items.name: Tao Kua Jao Kao Talat Sap Sin (Songkhla City)
items.blurb: Tao kua inside Talat Sap Sin market in central Songkhla — a breakfast spot for people who live here. The plate is generous and the price is honest. The market atmosphere keeps things relaxed and neighbourhood-feel. Good to eat before walking the Old Town or heading down to Samila Beach.
items.meta: Talat Sap Sin, Songkhla City · open early morning–mid-morning

items.name: Tao Kua Pa Juab (Original) (Songkhla City)
items.blurb: Another well-known tao kua veteran inside Songkhla City that locals recognise immediately. Full set of toppings, consistent dressing, and pairs well with the pork bone noodles. Worth it if you want an old-school experience in a properly old-school shop.

items.name: Tao Kua Street Carts — Nakhon Nok / Nakhon Nai Rd Area (Songkhla Old Town)
items.blurb: Along the Nakhon Nok–Nakhon Nai stretch of the Old Town you'll find push carts and small stalls selling tao kua in bags. Cheap, quick, no seating needed. Pairs perfectly with a walk to see the street art murals scattered across the neighbourhood.
items.meta: Nakhon Nok–Nakhon Nai Rd, Songkhla Old Town · morning–mid-morning

blocks.title: Honest heads-up
blocks.html: Tao kua is primarily a morning-to-early-afternoon food. Popular shops often sell out before 2 pm, and many take a regular weekly day off — some close on Mondays. If you're making a special trip to a specific shop, check their Facebook page or call ahead. Don't roll up late afternoon and expect to find every stall fully stocked.

blocks.text: A Half-Morning Tao Kua Walk Through Songkhla Old Town

blocks.html: To get the most out of tao kua, pair it with a walk around Songkhla Old Town. The veteran shops sit along Nang Ngam Road and the Nakhon Nok–Nakhon Nai area — the same streets lined with street art murals and colonial shophouses. Here's a short half-morning plan.

blocks.label: Half Morning
blocks.title: Tao Kua Walk + Songkhla Old Town

items.activity: Start on Nang Ngam Road — tao kua at one of the veteran shops
items.note: Pa Iad or Pa Juab — arrive early for a full set of toppings and a shorter wait

items.activity: Stroll along Nang Ngam Road and Nakhon Nai Road, browse old shophouses and snack stalls
items.note: Pick up local sweets and old-school coffee from shops along the way

items.activity: Hunt for street art murals in the Nakhon Nok–Nakhon Nai area
items.note: Murals are scattered across multiple spots — great for photos. If you're hungry again, tao kua carts and snack stalls are nearby

items.activity: Finish with coffee or a dessert at an Old Town café
items.note: Rest up before heading to Samila Beach or Khao Tang Kuan in the afternoon

blocks.html: Half a morning gets you both a genuinely local meal and the atmosphere of the Old Town in a single loop. The distances are short — most spots are within walking range of each other. It's a light, low-effort start for your first day in Songkhla.

blocks.text: How Is Tao Kua Different from a Regular Vermicelli Yam?

items.name: It's all in the dressing
items.blurb: A standard vermicelli yam leads with sour and spicy. Tao kua uses toddy palm sugar dressing where sweet comes first, with salt and sour following behind.

items.name: A very specific set of toppings
items.blurb: Tao kua centres on fried tofu, crispy whole prawns, shrimp crackers, pig ear, and soft-boiled duck egg — a fixed combination unique to this dish.

items.name: Not spicy — accessible to everyone
items.blurb: Tao kua is the rare Southern Thai dish that kids and spice-avoiders can eat without worry. Very different from the chilli-forward heat of most yam dishes.

faq.a: Tao kua is a Songkhla-specific one-plate dish that looks something like a salad or a yam. It combines blanched rice vermicelli, bean sprouts, fried tofu, crispy whole prawns, shrimp crackers, boiled pork, pig ear, soft-boiled duck egg, and vegetables — all dressed with a toddy palm sugar sauce that's sweet, salty, and sour. It's genuinely local food that's hard to find outside the Songkhla area.

faq.q: Why does tao kua use toddy palm sugar?
faq.a: Because the dressing is what makes the dish. Old-school shops simmer toddy palm sugar and palm vinegar from palms grown around Songkhla Lake — the flavour is a naturally deep, fragrant sweetness that you can't get from refined sugar. That's what separates Songkhla tao kua from generic vermicelli salads and from imitations made elsewhere.

faq.q: Where's the best tao kua in Songkhla and Hat Yai?
faq.a: In Songkhla Old Town the names to look for are Pa Iad and Pa Juab on Nang Ngam Road. In Hat Yai try Pa Taew at Kim Yong Market, Jeh Eng on Samchai Road, or the Pa Iad branch on the Khlong R.5 canal. Most shops operate morning to early afternoon only.

faq.q: Is tao kua spicy? Is it easy to eat?
faq.a: Tao kua is not spicy at all. The dressing leads with sweet from toddy palm sugar, and the overall flavour is mild and rounded. Children, elderly family members, and anyone nervous about Southern Thai spice can eat it comfortably. If you want more heat, ask for dried chilli flakes or chilli vinegar on the side.

faq.q: How much does tao kua cost, and what time should you go?
faq.a: Prices are very reasonable — roughly THB 30–60 per plate or bag. Go in the morning; tao kua is primarily a breakfast and lunch food, and popular shops often sell out before 2 pm. Many take a fixed day off each week, so a quick check before you visit is worth it.
